Do any of you know how to = specify a data filter in the input file? I have a data file that = contains all habitat types, and I would like to perform a separate = analysis for each habitat using the data filter function. Using the windows interface I have specified: Data Selection Line Transect New Field =3D b1 This works well with the windows interface but it does not show in the = log, which may guide me to the syntax to be used in the input file. Thanks Rick Woodburn British Trust for Ornithology. ------=_NextPart_000_001C_01BF5789.A96B97C0 Content-Type: text/html; charset="iso-8859-1" Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

> > Hi Rick,
> >
> > I'm sending this one to the list in case others are interested in the data
> > formats used by the distance analysis engine, especially the commands to tell
> > the D3.5 engine about the flat-file format.
> >
> > My answers are interspersed among your questions.
> >
> > Cheers,
> >
> >  - Len

> > On Tue, 4 Jan 2000 20:24:34 -0000, Rick Woodburn wrote:
> >
>> > >Dear Len
>> > >
>> > >I have made good progress in using the analysis engine as a stand alone
>> > >program, using the input file. However, I am having problems working out the
>> > >syntax for the infile command.
>> > >
>> > >I have written a program to produce both hierarchical and flat formats.
>> > >Could you tell me the syntax to import each of the formats?
>> > >
>> > >My files look like this (same data shown):
>> > >
>> > >Hierarchical:
>> > >
>> > >stratum /label=EC71 ;
>> > >sample /effort=1.2 /label=NY0922 ;
>> > >0      0      0     ;
>> > >sample /effort=0.4 /label=NY5381 ;
>> > >0      0      0     ;
>> > >sample /effort=1.2 /label=NY5882 ;
>> > >0      0      0     ;
>> > >sample /effort=0.4 /label=NZ1064 ;
>> > >1      0      0     ;
>> > >sample /effort=0.4 /label=NZ1364 ;
>> > >6      2      0     ;
>> > >sample /effort=0.8 /label=NZ2681 ;
>> > >8      3      4     ;
>> > >stratum /label=EC72 ;
>> > >sample /effort=0.4 /label=SD9085 ;
>> > >0      0      0     ;
>> > >sample /effort=0.4 /label=SE0051 ;
>> > >1      2      0     ;
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >Flat:
>> > >
>> > >EC71;NY0922;1.2;b1;
>> > >EC71;NY5381;0.4;b1;
>> > >EC71;NY5882;1.2;b1;
>> > >EC71;NZ1064;0.4;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ1364;0.4;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ1364;0.4;b1;12.5

>> > >EC71;NZ1364;0.4;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ1364;0.4;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ1364;0.4;b1;62.5
>> > >EC71;NZ1364;0.4;b1;62.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;12.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;62.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;62.5
>> > >EC71;NZ2681;0.8;b1;62.5
>> > >EC72;SD9085;0.4;b1;
>> > >EC72;SE0051;0.4;b1;12.5
>> > >EC72;SE0051;0.4;b1;62.5
>> > >EC72;SE0051;0.4;b1;62.5
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >Where, for example;
>> > >EC72 is the region,
>> > >SE0051 is the sample,
>> > >0.4 is the effort (line length),
>> > >b1 is the habitat type (originally included for post-strat analysis)
>> > >62.5 is the midpoint in the distance group 25-100m.
>> > >
>> > >For the Hierarchical format I have used:
>> > >
>> > > Data;
>> > > Infile=XXXX.dat;
>> > > End;
>> > >
>> > > With these commands, Distance recognises the strata and calculates the
>> > >total effort correctly, but makes some mistakes with recognising
>> > >observations, throwing the whole calculation.
> >
> > I am not aware of any problems with the distance analysis engine recognizing
> > the hierarchical format, although this is only used the Distance 3.5 engine
> > when importing old D2.2 command files.  Remember that you need to tell
> > Distance that your data are in groups with the command
> >
> >    DISTANCE=PERP/INTERVALS=0, 25, 100, 250;
> >
> > (assuming these are the right cutpoints) in the OPTIONS section (and
> > therefore you don't need to use /INTERVALS in the DISTANCE command in the
> > ESTIMATE section).  The Distance command language takes a bit of getting used
> > to, I'm afraid (which is why we wrote the windows interface).  It's unlikely
> > that you'll be able to simply cut and paste from the Log section of the
> > interface without understanding what you're doing and get good results.  If
> > you are not sure, I suggest you download Distance 2.2 from the web site, and
> > the documentation file (a separate download) - then have a look at the D2.2
> > example files, and then try your command file under D2.2 to check it works
> > there.
> >
>> > >For the Flat format I have used;
>> > >
>> > > Data; /Structure=Flat;
>> > > Infile=XXXX.dat;
>> > > End;
>> > >
>> > > I assume that this does not work because the program needs to be told the
>> > >variable labels. Also is a declaration of the delimiter needed?
> >
> > For one thing, I think it will not work as you have a semicolon directly
> > after the Data command, which you don't need.
> >
> > For another, you won't be able to import the "habitat field" that you have in
> > your data file - post-stratification is done by the D3.5 interface, not the
> > analysis engine.
> >
> > Thirdly, your data needs to be Tab delimited, as the engine doesn't recognize
> > any other format.  (It's the interface that can cope with comma delimited,
> > etc).
> >
> > Below, I have included some information that Jeff Laake wrote about the flat
> > data structure and was included in the Distance 3.0 readme file (Distance 3.0
> > was the first version to use the flat file structure).  Note that unlike the
> > heirarchical data, you will have to enter the data as ungrouped and then
> > analyze it as grouped (using the /INTERVALS switch in the DISTANCE command
> > under ESTIMATE).  Hopefully this will answer your flat format questions.  If
> > not, let me know.
> >
> > Good luck!
> >
> > Abstract from Jeff's readme file:
> > ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
> > New Data Structure
> >         A new method of data entry has been added to v3.0.  The standard
> > hierarchical data structure in early versions is still accepted but a flat
> > file data structure has been added.  A /Structure switch has been added to
> > the Data command which takes the values Flat or Hierarchy (default).  Flat
> > file data entry enables easy access to data that are kept in spreadsheets or
> > databases by exporting the data into a file with tab-delimited fields. There
> > are 3 steps to using the flat file data structure:
> > 1) Create a file with the data fields delimited by tabs (most easily done
> > with a spreadsheet or database),
> > 2) Specify to DISTANCE the order of the data fields, using the FIELDS command
> > unless you have used the default order, and
> > 3) Specify to DISTANCE the name of the file containing the data, using the
> > INFILE command (keyboard entry is not allowed).
> > The flat file data structure is limited to entering ungrouped data, but
> > grouped data can be  entered ungrouped and analyzed as grouped.
> >
> > Creating the data file
> > Create a data file which has a record (line) for each observation (sighting)
> > and a record for any sample (line or point) without any observations.  Each
> > record should contain the following fields separated by tabs:
> > a) Distance data
> >       DISTANCE                 if TYPE=LINE and DIST=PERP
> >       DISTANCE                 if TYPE=POINT or CUE
> >       DISTANCE & ANGLE         if TYPE=LINE and DIST=RADIAL
> > b) Cluster size
> >       SIZE                     if OBJECT=CLUSTER
> > c) Sample data
> >       SMP_LABEL                required (up to 50 characters)
> >       SMP_EFFORT               required(except for default value of 1)
> > d) Stratum data (optional)
> >       STR_LABEL                optional (up to 50 characters)
> >       STR_AREA                 optional size of geographic region
> >                                    to compute abundance
> >
> > If there are no observations for a sample, the distance and cluster size data
> > should be left blank and only the sample/strata data given.  The records in
> > the file should be grouped by sample and stratum (if used) but they do not
> > need to be sorted by the label.  For example,
> >
> > Stratum    Sample      Distance
> > -------    ----------  --------
> > Str1  10   Sample1  1   10.3
> > Str1  10   Sample2  1                - no observation for this sample
> > Str2  10   Sample3  1   1.1
> > Str2  10   Sample4  1   5.5
> > Str2  10   Sample4  1   53.4
> >
> > The following ordering would incorrectly create 3 strata:
> > Stratum    Sample      Distance
> > -------    ----------  --------
> > Str1  10   Sample1  1   10.3
> > Str2  10   Sample3  1   1.1
> > Str2  10   Sample4  1   5.5
> > Str2  10   Sample4  1   53.4
> > Str1  10   Sample2  1                - no observation for this sample
> >
> > Sample and stratum data only need to be given on the first record identifying
> > the stratum or sample.  The correct example above could be given as:
> >
> > Stratum    Sample      Distance
> > -------    ----------  --------
> > Str1  10   Sample1  1   10.3
> >            Sample2  1                - no observation for this sample
> > Str2  10   Sample3  1   1.1
> >            Sample4  1   5.5
> >                         53.4
> >
> > Empty fields are indicated by adjoining tabs delimiting an empty field.  With
> > database software, an outer join between and sample and observation tables
> > will create the appropriate file structure. An outer join will create a
> > record for samples with no observations.
> >
> > Specifying the order of the fields:  The order of the fields within the
> > record can follow the default order of (STR_LABEL, STR_AREA, SMP_LABEL,
> > SMP_EFFORT, DISTANCE, ANGLE, SIZE) in which ANGLE and SIZE are only needed
> > under the appropriate conditions or the order can be specified to DISTANCE
> > with the FIELDS command.   The FIELDS command has the following syntax:
> >
> > FIELDS = fieldname1, fieldname2, ... ;
> >
> > where the fieldnames are from the following list and the order within the
> > list should match the order within the record:
> >
> > STR_LABEL, STR_AREA, SMP_LABEL, SMP_EFFORT, DISTANCE, ANGLE, SIZE
> >
> > Specifying the input filename: The data filename is specified with the INFILE
> > command which has the following syntax:
> >
> > INFILE = filename;
> >
> > ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >
>> > >
>> > >Thanks for any help that you can give.
>> > >Happy Y2K.
>> > >
>> > >Rick
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
> >
> > --
> > Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
> > Distance Development Project
> > Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
> > Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
> > Scotland KY16 9SS
> >
> >              email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
> >    RUWPA home page: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk
> > Distance home page: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

Abstract from Jeff's readme file:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
New Data Structure
	A new method of data entry has been added to v3.0.  The standard
hierarchical data structure in early versions is still accepted but a flat
file data structure has been added.  A /Structure switch has been added to
the Data command which takes the values Flat or Hierarchy (default).  Flat
file data entry enables easy access to data that are kept in spreadsheets or
databases by exporting the data into a file with tab-delimited fields. There
are 3 steps to using the flat file data structure:
1) Create a file with the data fields delimited by tabs (most easily done
with a spreadsheet or database),
2) Specify to DISTANCE the order of the data fields, using the FIELDS command
unless you have used the default order, and
3) Specify to DISTANCE the name of the file containing the data, using the
INFILE command (keyboard entry is not allowed).
The flat file data structure is limited to entering ungrouped data, but
grouped data can be  entered ungrouped and analyzed as grouped.

Creating the data file
Create a data file which has a record (line) for each observation (sighting)
and a record for any sample (line or point) without any observations.  Each
record should contain the following fields separated by tabs:
a) Distance data
      DISTANCE                 if TYPE=LINE and DIST=PERP
      DISTANCE                 if TYPE=POINT or CUE
      DISTANCE & ANGLE         if TYPE=LINE and DIST=RADIAL
b) Cluster size
      SIZE                     if OBJECT=CLUSTER
c) Sample data
      SMP_LABEL                required (up to 50 characters)
      SMP_EFFORT               required(except for default value of 1)
d) Stratum data (optional)
      STR_LABEL                optional (up to 50 characters)
      STR_AREA                 optional size of geographic region
                                   to compute abundance

If there are no observations for a sample, the distance and cluster size data
should be left blank and only the sample/strata data given.  The records in
the file should be grouped by sample and stratum (if used) but they do not
need to be sorted by the label.  For example,

Stratum    Sample      Distance
-------    ----------  --------
Str1  10   Sample1  1   10.3
Str1  10   Sample2  1                - no observation for this sample
Str2  10   Sample3  1   1.1
Str2  10   Sample4  1   5.5
Str2  10   Sample4  1   53.4

The following ordering would incorrectly create 3 strata:
Stratum    Sample      Distance
-------    ----------  --------
Str1  10   Sample1  1   10.3
Str2  10   Sample3  1   1.1
Str2  10   Sample4  1   5.5
Str2  10   Sample4  1   53.4
Str1  10   Sample2  1                - no observation for this sample

Sample and stratum data only need to be given on the first record identifying
the stratum or sample.  The correct example above could be given as:

Stratum    Sample      Distance
-------    ----------  --------
Str1  10   Sample1  1   10.3
           Sample2  1                - no observation for this sample
Str2  10   Sample3  1   1.1
           Sample4  1   5.5
                        53.4

Empty fields are indicated by adjoining tabs delimiting an empty field.  With
database software, an outer join between and sample and observation tables
will create the appropriate file structure. An outer join will create a
record for samples with no observations.

Specifying the order of the fields:  The order of the fields within the
record can follow the default order of (STR_LABEL, STR_AREA, SMP_LABEL,
SMP_EFFORT, DISTANCE, ANGLE, SIZE) in which ANGLE and SIZE are only needed
under the appropriate conditions or the order can be specified to DISTANCE
with the FIELDS command.   The FIELDS command has the following syntax:

FIELDS = fieldname1, fieldname2, ... ;

where the fieldnames are from the following list and the order within the
list should match the order within the record:

STR_LABEL, STR_AREA, SMP_LABEL, SMP_EFFORT, DISTANCE, ANGLE, SIZE

Specifying the input filename: The data filename is specified with the INFILE
command which has the following syntax:

INFILE = filename;

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

> >
> >Thanks for any help that you can give.
> >Happy Y2K.
> >
> >Rick
> >
> >
> >

messages.subject: Re: Sampling highly variable cluster sizes
messages.body_plain:
> > This is a quick logistical question from someone very new to the
distance sampling world. I am currently using both point and line
transects to monitor carnivore prey levels in the Serengeti, Tanzania. On
the whole this is a perfect environment for distance sampling with most
species in distinct groups and clear fields of view for relatively easy
distance estimation. However, when the migration moves through, the
entire methodology breaks down - clusters are no longer distinct and
therefore there is no easily definable centre-of-cluster to estimate a
distance to. The animals effectively form one giant cluster which usually
extends out of sight. At present, the best I can do is simply estimate
numbers of animals within certain distance bands, which means my
methodology changes according to prey concentration, which is not exactly
ideal. Does anyone have experience with such variable counting
conditions? If so I would greatly appreciate any advice.

Tom, I think the most practical option is to have pre-defined conditions
under which you switch from line transect sampling to strip transect
sampling, in which you just count number of animals within a defined
distance - chosen so that you can be reasonably confident of avoiding any
serious undercount of animals within the strip.  Conceptually, this isn't
really different methodology - it is a line transect sample with a uniform
detection function.  It does require use of a shorter truncation distance,
and it is likely to be impractical to estimate distances, so that you
can't check whether there is any fall-off in detctability.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: cluster estimation
messages.body_plain:
Tom:

The problem  you describe is similar to one I have encountered in applying
distance sampling methods for estimation of fish density in the shallow
littoral zone of lakes.  Cluster size (ie, school size) is highly variable
and at times beyond the capacity of anyone to count in a reasonable time
period.  Attempting to find the 'centre of gravity' for each school
(cluster) results in heaping closer to the line than is desirable.  In fact,
this heaping artifact (in addition to the obvious counting problem) is one
of the most subtle observer effects that persists in our survey work.
Observers just seem to locate these clusters closer to the line that they
should.  I've been at this sort of thing for a few years now and I still
have to work very carefully at avoiding this problem.  The solution that
I've come up with echoes Steve Buckland's comments.  When faced with certain
species or habitats where clusters are simply too big to handle we have gone
to using strip sampling to acquire density estimates.  In our case, earlier
work has provided good estimates of a detection function for individuals and
clusters of manageable size which we use to set our visible limits for the
supplementary strip method as a means of ensuring maximum detectability
across the strip.  We operate at a scale of meters but the principle should
be the same for you.

This topic is another good reason for Len to include some strip sampling
components in a future edition of Distance....(sorry Len!)

messages.body_plain:
This discussion is, I think, pertinent to a situation which I have encountered
in sampling birds using point transects in shrubland in Hong Kong.

Most detections are by vocalisation and a couple of species (both bulbuls) are
so common that beyond about 100m my ability to discriminate between individual
sources of calls for these species breaks down (I call it the "bulbul
babble"). The solution, of course, is to truncate, but this results in a
uniform detection function (ie there is no fall-off in detectability before
the truncation point). Since Distance is based on the assumption that I am
achieving 100% detection at the count point, then the corollary is that I am
also achieving 100% detection at the truncation point.

My concern is this (and apologies if this is blindingly obvious to others) -
if  the effect of truncation is to limit the section of the detection "curve"
to the shoulder where detection is 100%,  is there any value in using Distance
at all for these species other than the fact that it saves me from the bother
of calculating densities manually and it allows me to apply a uniform
treatment to all the bird species being sampled?

Mike Leven

On Mon, 24 Jan 2000 15:32:33 -0500, mark.r...@mnr.gov.on.ca wrote:

[...]

> >This topic is another good reason for Len to include some strip sampling
> >components in a future edition of Distance....(sorry Len!)

As you probably know, you can "fake" the current version of Distance into
doing strip transect analysis.  You do this by selecting a uniform detection
detection function and no adjustment terms (see my messages of 13th and 14th
December 1999 in the distance-sampling archives
http://www.mailbase.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling/archive.html).
This works even if the strip width varies by stratum; however it doesn't work
with a mix of line transects and strip transects, which is what Steve
Buckland suggested and Tom implements in his fish surveys.  I expect Tom does
the estimation for the two "survey modes" separately and then combines the
density estimates by hand, using the formulae in Chapter 3 of the Distance
Sampling book.

In fact, you can fake Distance into doing some kind of job of it for you, but
at the cost of some efficiency.  To do this, put your strip transects into
their own strata as before (with a separate stratum for each strip width if
you have more than one strip width depending on conditions), with the
distances recorded as the distance to the strip boundary.  Then choose your
favourite detection function and adjustment term for your line transect data,
and ask Distance to estimate density by stratum.  What happens?  Distance
fits the detection function as normal to your line transect data.  But in the
strata that contain the strip transect data, it fits a straight line as this
is the most parsimonious fit it can find (it can't fit an increasing
function, which is what it would like to do, because of the constraint that
the function must be non-increasing).  The downside is that it is estimating
some parameters for these strip transect strata that it doesn't need to, so
you will loose some precision.  Also the AIC is garbage as are the goodness-
of-fits in the strip transect strata.  The upside is that you don't have to
get your calculator out and work out the density by hand.  Your choice.

Basically though, Tom is right.  I should try to incorporate mixed strip/line
transect designs into Distance 4.  Given my current schedule, it may not be
in 4.0, but we'll try and get it in at some point...

distances recorded as the distance to the strip boundary.  Then choose your
favourite detection function and adjustment term for your line transect data,
and ask Distance to estimate density by stratum.  What happens?  Distance
fits the detection function as normal to your line transect data.  But in the
strata that contain the strip transect data, it fits a straight line as this
is the most parsimonious fit it can find (it can't fit an increasing
function, which is what it would like to do, because of the constraint that
the function must be non-increasing).  The downside is that it is estimating
some parameters for these strip transect strata that it doesn't need to, so
you will loose some precision.  Also the AIC is garbage as are the goodness-
of-fits in the strip transect strata.  The upside is that you don't have to
get your calculator out and work out the density by hand.  Your choice.

Basically though, Tom is right.  I should try to incorporate mixed strip/line
transect designs into Distance 4.  Given my current schedule, it may not be
in 4.0, but we'll try and get it in at some point...

messages.body_plain:
-------------------------------------------------
               INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON DISTANCE SAMPLING
                    Estimating wildlife abundance for
                   Ecology, Management and Conservation

                         July 30 - August 3 2001
                          St. Andrews, Scotland

                     http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/icods/
             -------------------------------------------------
                         PRELIMINARY ANNOUNCEMENT
             -------------------------------------------------

Invitation
----------

We invite you to participate in the first International Conference on
Distance Sampling, to be held on July 30 - August 3 2001 in St. Andrews,
Scotland.  This announcement contains preliminary information about the
conference.  Please visit our web site for more details and to register
interest in attending.

Objectives
----------

The aim of this conference is to bring together for the first time all those
interested in the estimation of wildlife abundance using distance sampling
methods. Determining the density or abundance of wildlife populations is a
key component of population ecology, wildlife management and biological
conservation. For many taxa, distance sampling methods such as line
transects, point transects (variable circular plots) and trapping webs are
the most efficient approach.  These methods are now in very widespread use by
biologists, and there have been many recent developments in the underlying
theory that increase the scope of the methods.  The time is right for a major
international gathering.

Our major objectives are to:

-Bring together practitioners from a wide range of disciplines and systems,
as well as statisticians involved in methodological development

-Present examples of new research and best practice through invited plenary
talks

-Provide a forum for the exchange of ideas, techniques and methods through
contributed talks, posters and informal discussion sessions

-Provide world-class training for those new to the subject, through linked
workshops to be held before the conference

We hope that the conference will prove to be a major milestone in the
application of wildlife survey techniques, producing a quantum leap in the
effectiveness of field studies and stimulating many new areas of research.

Conference program
------------------

The conference will be a mix of plenary papers, giving state of the art
reviews of theory and practice, and contributed papers and posters.  In
addition, meeting rooms will be available for delegates to schedule and
attend informal discussion groups on topics of their choice.

The following leading experts in the field have agreed to give plenary paper.
(The preliminary topic of their paper is given in brackets.)

- David R. Anderson
  Colorado Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, Colorado, USA
  (Passive sampling and remote detection of objects: trapping webs,
  cameras and other extensions.)

- Colin Bibby
  Birdlife International, Cambridge, UK
  (Estimation of bird abundance and its relevance to conservation.)

- David L. Borchers
  University of St Andrews, UK
  (Unified models for estimating wildlife abundance.)

- Stephen T. Buckland
  University of St Andrews, UK
  (Overview of research linked to the Distance4 project.)

- Kenneth P.  Burnham
  Colorado Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, Colorado, USA
  (Large scale, long term monitoring.)

- Jeffrey L. Laake
  National Marine Mammal Lab, Seattle, USA
  (TBA)

- Bryan F.J. Manly
  University of Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand
  (Simultaneous estimation of population size and habitat selection by
  distance sampling.)

- Kenneth H. Pollock
  North Carolina State University, USA
  (Combining capture recapture and distance sampling, or Comparisons of
  detectability estimation methods for circular plots on birds.)

- Fred L. Ramsey
  Oregon State University, USA
  (A general paradigm for all variable area survey procedures.)

In addition, we are planning field trips and a full social program.

Further information
-------------------

More information about the conference, including a form for registering
interest, is at the conference web site:
